$comment: Shared conformance vectors for the gcache JSON value envelope.
Read by BOTH tests/test_conformance.py and packages/gcache-ts/test/gcache-conformance.test.ts.
Neither suite may hardcode these cases: the point is one source of truth, so a reader that
diverges fails rather than passing against its own mirrored copy.
Why this file exists. Parity between the Python and TypeScript readers used to be asserted
by hand-mirrored literals in two suites that run in separate CI workflows, so a divergence
was only ever caught by a human reading both. Two escaped that way and were found in
review, not by a test: an empty urn_prefix (Python omits the component, TS joins it) and a
fractional timestamp (TS kept the fraction, Python rounded, and the comparison is against a
threshold so the boolean flipped). Both are in here now as vectors.
expect=accept means decode succeeds AND yields `decoded`. expect=reject means the reader
must treat the value as a MISS -- an exception both clients convert to 'miss', never a
partial or defaulted value. A reject case with a plausible-looking payload is deliberate:
expect=accept means decode succeeds AND yields `decoded`. expect=reject means the reader
must treat the value as a MISS -- an exception both clients convert to 'miss', never a
partial or defaulted value. A reject case with a plausible-looking payload is deliberate:
a reader that ignores the invalid field and returns the payload anyway must fail here.
A vector may carry `rejectedBy`/`acceptedBy` when the clients DELIBERATELY differ. That is
not a divergence bug: it means one client cannot represent the value faithfully and
rejecting it there produces a miss-and-rewrite, which is strictly better than two clients
serving the same bytes as different numbers. `asymmetryIsSafe` must say why the direction
is the safe one. A suite only asserts the cases that apply to its own client.

vectors.name: canonical
vectors.why: The shape both writers emit. If this fails nothing else matters.

vectors.name: whole-number-float-timestamps
vectors.why: 1757308800123.0 IS a whole number of milliseconds. Rejecting every float would be over-strict, and this vector is what keeps the is_integer/isInteger check from degenerating into that.

vectors.name: fractional-expires
vectors.why: Found in review, not by a test. TS kept the fraction and Python rounded; both compare against a threshold, so expiresAtMs=x.9 at now=x is a HIT in one client and EXPIRED in the other. Same bytes, opposite answers -- so both must reject.

vectors.name: fractional-created
vectors.why: Same divergence on the other field, which feeds `watermark_ms >= createdAtMs` rather than expiry. Both fields need the vector; fixing one and not the other passed a single-field test.

vectors.name: negative-fractional-created
vectors.why: int() truncates toward zero and floor does not, so the two rounding strategies disagree in OPPOSITE directions for a negative value. That sign dependence is why rounding was the wrong fix at all.

vectors.name: version-zero
vectors.why: Not the current version, so not readable. Pinned because `version` was once checked truthily, which accepted 0.

vectors.name: version-true
vectors.why: JSON true is not 1. Python's `version != 1` is False for True because bool is an int subclass, so it was ACCEPTED there and rejected in TS -- a divergence with no symptom until a foreign writer produced one.

vectors.name: created-at-string
vectors.why: A timestamp as a string is the most likely shape from a hand-written or foreign entry. Must be a miss, not a coerced number.

vectors.name: expires-beyond-double
vectors.why: A 401-digit integer literal. JSON.parse maps it to Infinity so TS rejected it, while Python's arbitrary-precision int accepted it happily -- and an entry with an impossible expiry never looks expired AND can never satisfy watermark_ms >= createdAtMs, so no invalidation can ever reach it.

vectors.name: base64-payload
vectors.why: The bytes path. Python base64s a bytes payload where Go never does, so this is the one encoding both must agree on.

vectors.name: unknown-encoding
vectors.why: An encoding neither client implements must miss rather than being read as utf8.

vectors.name: payload-not-a-string
vectors.why: The payload is a JSON string carrying serialized bytes, never a nested object. A reader that accepts an object here would re-serialize it differently from the writer.

vectors.name: missing-expires
vectors.why: An absent expiry is not an infinite one.

vectors.name: not-json-at-all
vectors.why: Garbage in the keyspace must be a miss, never an exception that escapes the read path -- a cache must not be able to fail a request.

vectors.name: created-above-2-53
vectors.why: The silent-disagreement case, and the reason isInteger was not enough. JSON.parse rounds 9007199254740993 to 9007199254740992, which IS integral -- so TS accepted it while Python read the exact value and Go decoded it inside int64. All three then ACCEPT and disagree about the number, with the watermark comparison resolving differently on either side of 2^53 and no error anywhere. Worse than a miss.
vectors.asymmetryIsSafe: TS is stricter here on purpose. It rejects exactly the range it cannot represent faithfully, so the entry misses and is rewritten in a form all three agree about -- rather than being served with two different values. Python and Go accept up to int64, which libs/go/gcache/envelope.go already documents as the safe direction. No legitimate writer reaches it: real timestamps are ~1.7e12 and 2^53 ms is year 287396.

vectors.name: created-at-max-safe-integer
vectors.why: The boundary itself, so the safe-integer check cannot drift into rejecting the largest faithfully-representable value. 9007199254740991 is Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER and every client reads it exactly.

$comment: Key grammar, which is where the OTHER divergence lives. These are not decode vectors;
they record what each client renders today so a change to either is visible here.
TS percent-encodes every component via encodeURIComponent (key.ts joinUrnComponents);
Python interpolates raw. That is a known defect with a follow-up.
The empty-prefix row is different in kind: it is the one case that SURVIVES fixing the
encoding, because the divergence is structural -- Python omits the component, TS joins
it. That is why gcache now raises EmptyUrnPrefixNotSupported instead of documenting it.

cases.name: namespaced-prefix
cases.reason: TS percent-encodes the prefix. A namespaced prefix is the normal case and contains colons, so this is the common path, not an edge case. Known defect, follow-up filed against the encoding.

cases.name: empty-prefix
cases.reason: Structural, not an encoding choice: Python omits an empty component, TS joins it. Survives the encoding fix, so gcache rejects this configuration at construction (EmptyUrnPrefixNotSupported) rather than documenting it.
